question.text: Can infundibular height predict the clearance of lower pole calyceal stone after extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy?
question.context: To evaluate the efficacy of extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) on lower calyceal calculi in relation to the renal anatomical factors and determine which of these factors can be used to select patients who will benefit from SWL. We analyzed retrospectively 78 patients with single radiopaque lower calyceal stones treated with SWL. The patients were evaluated 3 months after lithotripsy with a simple abdominal X-ray and a kidney ultrasound scan. The success of the treatment, removal of all fragments, was correlated with renal anatomical factors measured in the pre-treatment intravenous urography: infundibulopelvic angle, lower infundibulum width, lower infundibulum length, ratio length/width, infundibulum height, and number of minor calyces in the lower calyceal group. Three months after SWL treatment, 39 patients were stone-free (NR group) and 39 had residual fragments (R group). Both groups presented no differences in relation to infundibulopelvic angle, width and length of the lower calyceal infundibulum, length/width ratio of the lower infundibulum or number of lower calyces. Height of the infundibulum, described as the distance between the line passing through the lowest part of the calyx containing the calculus and the highest point of the lower lip of renal pelvis, was the only parameter in which significant differences (p = 0.002) were found between the NR and R groups.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a statistically significant difference in infundibulum height between patients who achieved stone-free status after SWL and those with residual fragments. This suggests that infundibulum height may be a predictive factor for SWL success in lower calyceal stones.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The study found a significant difference in infundibulum height (p = 0.002) between the NR and R groups.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other anatomical factors were considered, infundibulum height was the only one that showed a significant difference in the study. Other factors like infundibulopelvic angle, width, length, and the number of minor calyces did not show significant differences, making infundibulum height the most relevant factor.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that infundibular height was the only parameter showing significant differences (p = 0.002) between the stone-free (NR) and residual fragment (R) groups. This suggests that infundibular height can predict the clearance of lower pole calyceal stones after SWL. The other measured parameters showed no significant differences between groups, making infundibular height the most reliable predictor.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Infundibular height showed significant differences (p = 0.002) between the NR and R groups, while other parameters did not.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed to be considered as the question specifically asks about the predictive value of infundibular height for SWL success, not about differential diagnoses.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that infundibular height was the only anatomical parameter with statistically significant difference (p=0.002) between stone-free (NR) and residual stone (R) groups, indicating it can predict SWL success. All other anatomical factors showed no significant difference between groups.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Infundibular height was the only parameter with significant difference (p=0.002) between NR and R groups, suggesting it predicts clearance of lower pole calyceal stones after SWL.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other anatomical parameters (angle, width, length, ratio, number of calyces) were considered but ruled out as predictors due to lack of statistical significance between groups.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Significant difference in infundibular height between the stone-free and residual fragment groups.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible factors such as stone size, location within the calyx, or patient-specific variables (e.g., renal function, stone composition) could theoretically influence SWL outcome, but the study found no differences in these. The only significant predictor in the data was infundibular height, indicating a possible association but not a guaranteed predictor.
